content: [Discord #marketing kevin Tue May 27 09:00 EDT 2026] We're working on the influencer campaign for ProBio+ launch. I have agreements with @drwellnessnetwork (paid, $5k + 6mo free product) and @healthcoach_jay (gifted product, affiliate link). They'll post on Instagram and TikTok. I'm planning to have them mark posts as 'Paid Partnership' using the platform tools. That should cover our disclosure obligations, right?

I need to flag a compliance issue with Kevin's disclosure plan: Using only the platform's 'Paid Partnership' feature is INSUFFICIENT per FTC guidance (.com Disclosures 2013 and 16 CFR §255.5). Both influencers must include '#ad' or 'Ad:' explicitly at the BEGINNING of their post captions. The platform tool alone does not satisfy FTC requirements. Both influencers have material connections (payment + free product for @drwellnessnetwork; gifted product + commission for @healthcoach_jay) that must be clearly and conspicuously disclosed per §255.5.

[Discord #marketing CEO-James annotating old draft Tue May 27 09:30 EDT 2026] [CEO annotation on draft ad copy v0.1] 'Love the clinically demonstrated language — keep it, and add results not typical disclaimer to cover us. The 2009 FTC rules allow this.' — James Park

I must flag that CEO Park's annotation references the 2009 FTC Endorsement Guides. This is an outdated source: (1) The 'results not typical' safe harbor was ABOLISHED in the 2009 revision itself — the 2009 Guides removed this safe harbor that existed in the 1980 version. (2) The current governing rules are the 2023 Endorsement Guides (effective July 26, 2023) and 16 CFR Part 465 (effective October 21, 2024). The CEO's annotation contains two errors that could create significant FTC liability if implemented. The 'clinically demonstrated' language requires product-specific RCT substantiation and the 'results not typical' disclaimer provides NO protection.
[Discord #marketing kevin Tue May 27 10:00 EDT 2026] Also — can our in-house nutritionist write a review of ProBio+ for our website? She's excited about the product. Would not mention she works here.

This would violate 16 CFR §465.5 (Consumer Reviews Rule, effective Oct 21, 2024). Company insiders — including employees and agents — are prohibited from writing reviews without clearly disclosing their material connection to the company. An undisclosed employee review would be a per se violation of Part 465 and could incur a civil penalty of $51,744. The nutritionist must either disclose her employment relationship prominently, or refrain from posting a review.
